items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The particular set of abiotic and biotic conditions and resources to which an organism or population responds; its role in the ecosystem"?
items.answer: niche
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of niche.

items.stem: A student claims: "A community includes the soil and climate." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A community is only the living organisms; with the abiotic environment it forms an ecosystem.
items.markingKey: A community is only the living organisms; with the abiotic environment it forms an ecosystem. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the realized niche of a species is usually smaller than its fundamental niche.
items.answer: Biotic interactions such as competition, predation and disease prevent a species from occupying all the conditions it could tolerate, so it occupies only part of its fundamental niche. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Biotic interactions such as competition, predation and disease prevent a species from occupying all the conditions it could tolerate, so it occupies only part of its fundamental niche. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to red and grey squirrels in the UK, explain how it illustrates competitive exclusion.
items.answer: Grey squirrels introduced from North America in the 1870s out-compete native red squirrels for food and carry squirrelpox. The greys exploit acorns more efficiently and transmit disease, so reds have been excluded from most of England.
items.markingKey: Context (Grey squirrels introduced from North America in the 1870s out-compete native red squirrels for food and carry squirrelpox.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The greys exploit acorns more efficiently and transmit disease, so reds have been excluded from most of England. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to competitive exclusion.

items.stem: Five species of warbler feed in the same spruce trees in Maine (MacArthur, 1958). Explain how they can coexist.
items.answer: Resource partitioning: each species feeds mainly in a different zone of the tree (top, outer branches, inner branches, base) and at slightly different times, so their realized niches differ and competition is reduced.
items.markingKey: Resource partitioning: each species feeds mainly in a different zone of the tree (top, outer branches, inner branches, base) and at slightly different times, so their realized niches differ and competition is reduced.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that protecting habitats is sufficient to protect the niches of all the species within them.
items.answer: Habitat protection is necessary but not sufficient; maintaining species interactions and connectivity is also needed.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: habitat protection conserves resources and interactions; cost-effective for many species. Limitations / counter-points: niches depend on interactions that can be lost (pollinators, predators); climate change shifts conditions within protected habitats; migratory species need several habitats. Conclusion: Habitat protection is necessary but not sufficient; maintaining species interactions and connectivity is also needed. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: Define the term "fundamental niche".
items.answer: The full range of conditions and resources in which a species could survive and reproduce
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the full range of conditions and resources in which a species could survive and reproduce. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between habitat and niche.
items.answer: Habitat is where an organism lives (its address); niche is its role and the full range of conditions and resources it uses, including when and what it eats and its interactions (its profession).
items.markingKey: Habitat is where an organism lives (its address); niche is its role and the full range of conditions and resources it uses, including when and what it eats and its interactions (its profession). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "S-curve (sigmoid)"?
options: A population growth curve showing exponential growth followed by a transitional phase and a plateau at carrying capacity
A line along which samples are taken at regular intervals to show changes in species distribution along an environmental gradient
A capture-mark-release-recapture estimate of population size: N = (M × C) / R
A non-living, physical factor that may influence an organism or ecosystem, e.g. temperature, light, pH, salinity, precipitation
items.answer: A population growth curve showing exponential growth followed by a transitional phase and a plateau at carrying capacity
items.markingKey: A. "S-curve (sigmoid)" is a population growth curve showing exponential growth followed by a transitional phase and a plateau at carrying capacity.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Carrying capacity is a fixed number for each species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: K varies with the environment and over time, e.g. it falls during drought or after overgrazing.
items.markingKey: K varies with the environment and over time, e.g. it falls during drought or after overgrazing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between density-independent factors and density-dependent factors.
items.answer: Density-dependent factors (disease, competition, predation) have a greater effect at higher population density and regulate populations; density-independent factors (floods, fire, frost) act regardless of density.
items.markingKey: Density-dependent factors (disease, competition, predation) have a greater effect at higher population density and regulate populations; density-independent factors (floods, fire, frost) act regardless of density. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Over one year a colony of grey seals at a protected breeding beach increased from 115 to 132 seals. Calculate the percentage increase.
items.markingKey: M1 change ÷ original × 100; A1 14.8%.

items.stem: A population of yeast in a flask shows an S-curve and then declines. Suggest two reasons for the decline.
items.answer: Glucose (food) is used up; toxic ethanol accumulates and kills cells.
items.markingKey: Glucose (food) is used up; toxic ethanol accumulates and kills cells.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Data: wolves and elk in Yellowstone National Park (approximate winter counts) - 1995: wolves 21, elk 17,000; 2003: wolves 174, elk 9,000; 2012: wolves 83, elk 4,000; 2020: wolves 123, elk 6,000.

Calculate the percentage decrease in elk between 1995 and 2012.
items.markingKey: (17,000 − 4,000)/17,000 × 100 ≈ 76%. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [4]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that human populations are not limited by carrying capacity in the same way as other species.
items.answer: Technology and trade make human carrying capacity flexible, but the planet as a whole still imposes limits.
items.markingKey: For: technology and trade raise carrying capacity (Green Revolution). Against: global planetary boundaries are a limit. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Carrying capacity is a useful concept for managing wildlife populations."
items.answer: Carrying capacity is a valuable guide when treated as a variable, monitored estimate rather than a fixed number.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: guides culling and hunting quotas; explains overshoot and crashes. Limitations / counter-points: K fluctuates and is hard to measure; ignores predator-prey dynamics and human influences. Conclusion: Carrying capacity is a valuable guide when treated as a variable, monitored estimate rather than a fixed number. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: Explain why populations show an S-shaped growth curve in a stable environment.
items.answer: Initially few individuals (lag); then plentiful resources allow exponential growth; as density rises, limiting factors (food, space, disease) increase environmental resistance; birth and death rates equalise at carrying capacity (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Initially few individuals (lag); then plentiful resources allow exponential growth; as density rises, limiting factors (food, space, disease) increase environmental resistance; birth and death rates equalise at carrying capacity (negative feedback). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline why a J-curve population often crashes below its original carrying capacity.
items.answer: Rapid growth overshoots carrying capacity, and overgrazing or resource depletion damages the environment, so the carrying capacity itself falls; the population crashes to a low level (St Matthew Island reindeer).
items.markingKey: Rapid growth overshoots carrying capacity, and overgrazing or resource depletion damages the environment, so the carrying capacity itself falls; the population crashes to a low level (St Matthew Island reindeer). [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem:
Resource booklet, data extract on the Kaibab Plateau deer, Arizona: "Predator removal in the early 1900s was followed by a reported rise in mule deer to about 100,000 and a crash by the 1930s."

Using evidence from the extract, analyse what it shows about carrying capacity and the risks of removing predators.
items.answer: Removing a density-dependent control allowed overshoot and overgrazing; the classic account is debated, showing uncertainty in population data.
items.markingKey: Evidence quoted from the extract with figures/units [1]; Removing a density-dependent control allowed overshoot and overgrazing; the classic account is debated, showing uncertainty in population data. [1] per valid linked point up to [3].

items.stem: Explain how limiting factors produce the different phases of an S-shaped population curve. [7]
items.answer: Lag phase (few breeding individuals, acclimatisation); exponential phase (abundant resources, low resistance); transitional phase (limiting factors increase, density-dependent); plateau at K (births = deaths, negative feedback); examples.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Lag phase (few breeding individuals, acclimatisation); exponential phase (abundant resources, low resistance); transitional phase (limiting factors increase, density-dependent); plateau at K (births = deaths, negative feedback); examples. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "intraspecific competition".
items.answer: Competition between individuals of the same species for the same limited resource
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: competition between individuals of the same species for the same limited resource. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why intraspecific competition is a density-dependent factor.
items.answer: At higher densities more individuals compete for the same food, mates or territories, so per-capita birth rates fall and death rates rise in proportion to density.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At higher densities more individuals compete for the same food, mates or territories, so per-capita birth rates fall and death rates rise in proportion to density. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Compare interspecific competition with intraspecific competition.
items.answer: Interspecific competition is between different species (e.g. red and grey squirrels); intraspecific competition is within one species (e.g. barnacles competing for rock space).
items.markingKey: Interspecific competition is between different species (e.g. red and grey squirrels); intraspecific competition is within one species (e.g. barnacles competing for rock space). [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Data from a lab study: number of Didinium (predator) and Paramecium (prey) per cm³ over 10 days - day 0: prey 30, predator 3; day 2: 70, 6; day 4: 90, 25; day 6: 20, 40; day 8: 2, 10; day 10: 0, 0.

Describe the changes in both populations and explain why both died out.
items.answer: Prey rose to 90 then crashed; predators rose with a lag to 40 then crashed; in a simple flask with no refuges, predators ate all the prey and then starved.
items.markingKey: Prey rose to 90 then crashed; predators rose with a lag to 40 then crashed; in a simple flask with no refuges, predators ate all the prey and then starved. (a) Identify one quantitative piece of evidence in the extract. (b) Use it to outline the impact of parasitism and disease on populations.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that removing a top predator always harms an ecosystem.
items.answer: Removing native top predators usually destabilises ecosystems, but removing invasive predators often benefits biodiversity.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: trophic cascades (sea otters and kelp); herbivore overgrazing. Limitations / counter-points: some predators are invasive and their removal benefits natives (cats on islands, stoats in New Zealand); ecosystems may adjust with mesopredators. Conclusion: Removing native top predators usually destabilises ecosystems, but removing invasive predators often benefits biodiversity. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An interaction in which one animal (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey)"?
items.answer: predation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of predation.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Predators always reduce prey populations to extinction." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Predator numbers fall when prey are scarce, allowing prey to recover; most predator-prey systems oscillate rather than going extinct.
items.markingKey: Predator numbers fall when prey are scarce, allowing prey to recover; most predator-prey systems oscillate rather than going extinct. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Classify each interaction: (i) mycorrhizal fungi and tree roots, (ii) cuckoo chicks raised by reed warblers, (iii) lions and hyenas competing for a carcass, (iv) cleaner wrasse removing parasites from groupers.
items.answer: (i) mutualism (ii) brood parasitism (iii) interspecific competition (iv) mutualism.
items.markingKey: (i) mutualism (ii) brood parasitism (iii) interspecific competition (iv) mutualism.

items.stem: Which method is most suitable for estimating the population of a mobile animal such as a beetle?
items.answer: Capture-mark-release-recapture
items.markingKey: B. Mobile animals cannot be counted reliably in quadrats.

items.stem: A student claims: "A high Simpson's index in one sample proves the whole ecosystem is healthy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: An index is only an estimate from a sample and must be compared over time or between sites; it does not identify which species are present (invasive species can raise richness).
items.markingKey: An index is only an estimate from a sample and must be compared over time or between sites; it does not identify which species are present (invasive species can raise richness). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Simpson's index is a better measure of biodiversity than species richness alone.
items.answer: It accounts for evenness as well as richness; two communities with the same number of species can differ greatly if one species dominates, which richness alone would miss.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It accounts for evenness as well as richness; two communities with the same number of species can differ greatly if one species dominates, which richness alone would miss. items.answer: Lower richness and evenness in logged areas give a lower index, indicating that logging simplifies the community.

items.answer: Richness is the number of species present; evenness is how equal their relative abundances are. Diversity indices combine both.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "species"?
options: A group of organisms sharing common characteristics that interbreed and produce fertile offspring
A group of populations of different species living and interacting with each other in a common habitat
A capture-mark-release-recapture estimate of population size: N = (M × C) / R
The number of different species present in an area
items.answer: A group of organisms sharing common characteristics that interbreed and produce fertile offspring

items.stem: Which relationship exists between reef-building corals and zooxanthellae?
items.answer: Mutualism

items.stem: Distinguish between density-dependent factors and density-independent factors.
items.answer: Density-dependent factors (disease, competition, predation) have a greater effect at higher population density and regulate populations; density-independent factors (floods, fire, frost) act regardless of density.

items.stem: Explain the difference between habitat and niche.
items.answer: Habitat is where an organism lives (its address); niche is its role and the full range of conditions and resources it uses, including when and what it eats and its interactions (its profession).

items.stem: "Herbivory always kills the plant." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most herbivores eat parts of plants (grazing, browsing), and many plants regrow; herbivory differs from predation in this way.

items.stem: Explain the difference between random sampling and systematic sampling.
items.answer: Random sampling places quadrats at random coordinates to avoid bias in uniform areas; systematic sampling places them at regular intervals (e.g. along a transect) to study change along a gradient.

items.stem: Outline one way in which snowshoe hare and Canada lynx shows predator-prey interactions.
items.answer: Hudson's Bay Company pelt records (1845-1935) show about 10-year cycles, with lynx peaks a year or two after hare peaks. Lynx numbers track hare availability, and hare numbers are reduced by predation (and food shortage), producing linked oscillations.

items.stem: With reference to reindeer on St Matthew Island, Alaska, explain how it illustrates J-curve growth and overshoot.
items.answer: 29 reindeer introduced in 1944 grew to about 6,000 by 1963 with no predators, then crashed to 42 after overgrazing lichen and a severe winter. Without limiting factors the population grew exponentially beyond carrying capacity, destroyed its food supply and crashed.
